passages.original: rebus editis laederentur. scis enim ipse tales 2 homines cum iis qui aliqua de maioribus eorum scripserat quantum gerant bellum, nec ignota esse arbitror quae dixit Marcus Tullius in Hortensio, quem ad exemplum Protreptici scripsit, unum tamen ponam, quod iucunditatem quandam sed vulgarem habuit, morem tamen novum fecit, nam cum cingula sua plerique militantium, qui ad convivium venerant, ponerent hora convivii, Saloninus puer sive Gallienus his auratos costilatosque balteos rapuisse perhibetur, et, cum esset difficile in aula Palatina requirere quod perisset, ac taciti ex militibus viri detrimenta pertulissent, postea rogati ad convivium cincti adcubuerunt, cumque ab his quaereretur, cur non solverent cingulum, respondisse dicuntur, Salonino deferimus, atque hinc tractum morem, ut deinceps cum imperatore cincti discumberent.
passages.english: ... would be harmed by the things published. For you know yourself how great a war such men wage against those who have written anything about their ancestors, and I do not think you are unaware of what Marcus Tullius said in the Hortensius, which he wrote on the model of the Protrepticus. I shall, however, set down one [story], which had a certain charm, though a common sort, yet it created a new custom. For when most of the soldiers who had come to a banquet were laying aside their belts at the hour of the banquet, the boy Saloninus, or Gallienus, is said to have snatched away their gilded and ribbed sword-belts; and since it was difficult in the Palatine court to search for what had been lost, and the soldiers had silently put up with the losses, afterwards, when invited to a banquet, they reclined at table with their belts on; and when they were asked why they did not undo their belts, they are said to have replied, "We are deferring to Saloninus." And from this, [it is said], the custom was drawn that thereafter they reclined at table with the emperor with their belts on.
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence; the subject of 'would be harmed' is in the lost preceding text. 'scripserat' (singular) after 'iis qui' is grammatically odd, perhaps for 'scripserint'; translated as plural. 'costilatos' is a rare word, taken as 'ribbed' or 'studded' (perhaps related to costa, 'rib'); the exact sense is uncertain. 'Salonino deferimus' could also mean 'we are saving [them] from Saloninus' or 'we are reporting [it] to Saloninus'. The joke turns on this word.
